title: Teaching: collar and clearing the C-spine
stem: Teaching room. A junior doctor asks you how to size and apply a cervical collar, and how to decide whether a patient's neck can be cleared without imaging. Teach them, then work through two quick cases with them.

phases.title: Set the scene
phases.goal: Introduce yourself, the objectives, what Dr Lau knows already, and a plan.

phases.title: Teach
phases.goal: The collar by Peyton's steps; the rule at the whiteboard; the examination shown on Dr Lau.

phases.title: Apply
phases.goal: Dr Lau fits the collar himself, then works through two cases.

phases.title: Close
phases.goal: His view first, specific feedback, a teach-back, resources, questions.

review.text: Collars for everyone. Your notes put a rigid collar on every trauma patient at risk of neck injury. Current guidance uses 'spinal motion restriction': manual in-line stabilisation, blocks and minimal handling are the core, and a collar is one option. Leave it off an alert patient who walked or climbed out themselves, and loosen or remove it if it causes distress, airway problems or raised ICP.

notes:
Checked against the Canadian C-spine Rule (Stiell 2001, 2003), NEXUS (Hoffman 2000), NICE NG41 (Spinal injury: assessment and initial management, 2016) and NICE NG232 (head injury imaging), and the Faculty of Pre-Hospital Care consensus on spinal motion restriction (2018).

Collar (a Laerdal Stifneck Select, after its directions for use): with the head held in line, measure in finger breadths from the top of the shoulder (the trapezius, where the collar sits) to the bottom of the chin; on the collar, match that from the sizing mark to the bottom edge of the hard plastic (not the foam); set it and the chin support to that size, press both lock tabs, and bend it into shape. Lying flat, slide the rear panel behind the neck first, into the midline; bring the chin support up under the chin; hold the front in place, pull the collar round snug, and fasten. Never adjust it on the patient; too big pushes the head back. Check the fit. Blocks and tape complete immobilisation. Current consensus favours minimal handling and 'spinal motion restriction': collars can raise ICP, cause pressure sores and aspiration, and are no longer routine in every patient (for example, the self-extricating, ambulant patient). Your notes' indications and complications are correct. The difference: your notes put a rigid collar on every trauma patient at risk of a neck injury. Current guidance (ATLS 10th 'spinal motion restriction'; Faculty of Pre-Hospital Care consensus 2018) still protects the spine in these patients, but a collar is now one option, not automatic. Manual in-line stabilisation, head blocks and minimal handling are the core. A collar is not needed for an alert, ambulant patient who walked or climbed out themselves, and can be loosened or removed if it causes distress, airway problems or raised ICP. NICE NG41 still uses collars for patients who meet its immobilisation criteria, so a collar is never 'wrong'. Just don't say it is mandatory for everyone.

Clearance: in an alert (GCS 15), stable, sober adult, apply the Canadian C-spine Rule. High risk (age 65 or over, dangerous mechanism, or paraesthesia in the limbs) → image. Otherwise, any low-risk factor (simple rear-end collision, sitting up in the ED, ambulatory at any time, delayed onset of neck pain, no midline tenderness) allows range-of-motion testing: can rotate 45° left and right → cleared. NEXUS is an alternative (no midline tenderness, no intoxication, normal alertness, no focal deficit, no painful distracting injury). CT is the first-line imaging in adults (NICE). Your notes match this.

Teaching structure (2026-10-15, rebuilt on the user's review: "first the learning objectives, then what the student knows, then teach, then apply"): set the scene (introduce, two objectives, explore prior knowledge, tailor and outline the plan); teach (the collar by Peyton's four steps: demonstrate at real speed in silence, deconstruct with explanation, the learner talks the teacher through it; the rule at the whiteboard, linked to the NEXUS he knows; the bedside examination shown on Dr Lau: posterior midline first, then active rotation); apply (Peyton step 4: Dr Lau fits the collar while you watch; two cases in which he reasons and you question and confirm); close (self-assessment first, specific balanced feedback, teach-back, resources, questions, a next step). Everything hands-on is shown in 3D: the collar on a manikin step by step (in-line stabilisation from the head end throughout, earrings out, finger measurement, sizing in a drawn close-up, back then front, fit, blocks and tape), and the examination on Dr Lau with an arc showing 45 degrees.

Perfect script checked against the Canadian C-spine Rule, NICE NG41, a Peyton four-step checklist, an HKCEM-style set-dialogue-closure teaching scheme and a keyword scheme.

steps.label: Talk to Dr Lau
steps.hint: Set the scene: introduce yourself, the objectives, what he knows already, then a plan.

turns.line: Thanks for this. I get nervous about necks.

opts.t: Hi Dr Lau, I'm the ED registrar. We have about ten minutes and nobody needs us: shall we do this at the manikin?
opts.mark: Introduces themself, builds rapport and sets the scene

turns.line: What are we going to cover?

opts.t: Two objectives. By the end you'll be able to fit a cervical collar correctly, and use the Canadian C-spine Rule to decide whose neck can be cleared without imaging.

turns.line: Where do you want me to start?

opts.t: First tell me what you know already: have you fitted a collar, and how do you decide who needs imaging?
opts.r: I've read about NEXUS, but I've never fitted a collar, and I'm never sure when the collar can come off.

opts.t: Not at all: that's a good start. You'll see the collar done, then step by step, then you'll fit it yourself. Then we'll build on NEXUS with the Canadian rule, and you'll apply it to two patients.
opts.mark: Tailors the session to the learner and outlines a plan

steps.label: Teach the collar (Peyton's steps)
steps.hint: Show it at real speed in silence; then each step, explained; then he talks you through it.

body.intro: The manikin lies flat on the table, earrings in; a collar and head blocks beside it. Dr Lau watches. Teach it Peyton's way: choose below.

Step 1: demonstrate.t: Watch first: I'll fit it at real speed, without talking.
Step 1: demonstrate.r: In-line stabilisation, earrings off, measured, sized and locked, rear panel, front, checked, blocks and tape: done in under a minute.
Step 1: demonstrate.mark: Peyton step 1: demonstrates at real speed, in silence

Step 2: explain each step.t: Now step by step. First, manual in-line stabilisation: someone holds the head from the head end, and keeps holding it until the blocks and tape are on.
Step 2: explain each step.r: The head is held in line from the head end.

Step 2: explain each step.t: Jewellery off: earrings and necklaces, so nothing is caught under the collar.
With the head held in line, measure with your fingers flat: from the top of the shoulder, the trapezius where the collar will sit, to the bottom of the chin. Here it's three fingers.
Step 2: explain each step.r: Three fingers from the top of the shoulder to the chin.
Step 2: explain each step.mark: Measures the neck: top of the shoulder to the chin, in fingers

Step 2: explain each step.t: On the collar, the same three fingers: from the red sizing mark in the size window down to the bottom edge of the hard plastic, not the foam. Set it to that size, press both lock tabs, then bend it into shape.
Step 2: explain each step.r: Set to three fingers, locked both sides, bent into shape.
Step 2: explain each step.mark: Sizes the collar to the measurement, locks it and shapes it

Step 2: explain each step.t: Lying flat, the rear panel goes in first: slide it behind the neck from your side, flat along the couch, until it is in the midline. The head doesn't move.
Step 2: explain each step.r: The rear panel is behind the neck, in the midline, its tail showing on the far side; the head has not moved.
Step 2: explain each step.mark: Slides the rear panel behind the neck first

Step 2: explain each step.t: Bring the front round with the chin support under the chin. Hold the front in place, pull the tail round snug, and fasten the Velcro.
Step 2: explain each step.r: The chin sits on the chin support; pulled snug and fastened.
Step 2: explain each step.mark: Chin support under the chin; holds the front, pulls it snug, fastens it

Step 2: explain each step.t: Check the fit: the chin on the chin support, no gaps, the airway opening in the midline, the pulses still accessible. Too big pushes the head back; too small lets it bend forward.
Step 2: explain each step.r: A good fit: no gaps, the airway opening in the midline.

Step 2: explain each step.t: Then blocks and tape: head blocks, then tape across the forehead first, then the chin. Only now can the hands come off.
Step 2: explain each step.r: Blocks on; taped forehead, then chin; in-line stabilisation released.
Step 2: explain each step.mark: Blocks and tape, forehead then chin, before letting go

Step 3: the learner talks you through it.t: Now you talk me through each step, and I'll do exactly what you say.
Step 3: the learner talks you through it.r: Dr Lau: "Hold the head in line. Earrings off. Three fingers, shoulder to chin. Red mark to the bottom of the plastic, lock both sides, shape it. Rear panel behind the neck, chin support under the chin, pull it round and fasten. Check the fit. Blocks, tape the forehead, then the chin." All in order.
Step 3: the learner talks you through it.mark: Peyton step 3: the learner talks the teacher through it

steps.label: Teach the rule at the whiteboard
steps.hint: Why a collar at all; the three questions, drawn; then link it to the NEXUS he knows.

opts.t: First, the collar is only one part of spinal motion restriction: in-line stabilisation, blocks and minimal handling matter most. Leave the collar off an alert patient who walked out of the car, and loosen it if it causes distress or raised pressure.
opts.mark: Spinal motion restriction: who needs a collar, and its harms

opts.t: The Canadian C-spine Rule is for alert, stable adults, GCS 15, with a possible neck injury. It asks three questions, in order.
opts.mark: States who the rule applies to

opts.t: One: any high-risk factor? Age 65 or over, a dangerous mechanism such as a fall from a metre or five stairs, or tingling in the limbs. If yes, image: CT C-spine.

Two: any of the low-risk factors that make it safe to test movement? A simple rear-end collision, sitting up in the department, walking at any time, neck pain that came on later, or no midline tenderness. If none, image.
opts.mark: Low-risk factors make it safe to assess movement

opts.t: Three: active rotation. Can they turn the head 45 degrees to the left and to the right? If yes, the neck is cleared clinically: no imaging, collar off. If not, image.
opts.mark: Active rotation 45° each way clears the neck

opts.t: You know NEXUS: no midline tenderness, not intoxicated, normally alert, no focal deficit, no painful distracting injury. The Canadian rule is the more sensitive and the more specific of the two.
opts.mark: Links the new rule to what the learner knows (NEXUS)

steps.label: Show the examination on Dr Lau
steps.hint: Feel the midline first; only then ask him to turn his head.

body.intro: Dr Lau sits on the edge of the couch so you can show the examination on him.

Show the examination.t: First feel down the middle of the back of the neck, every spinous process: tenderness there means image, and no movement test.
Show the examination.mark: Shows palpation of the posterior midline

Show the examination.t: Only then: turn your head to the left, then to the right, as far as you can.
Show the examination.r: 45 degrees to each side, no pain: that is a pass.
Show the examination.mark: Shows active rotation to 45° each way

steps.label: Dr Lau fits the collar (Peyton step 4)
steps.hint: He does it; you watch, and feed back at the end.

body.intro: Dr Lau's turn: he fits the collar on the manikin while you watch.

Step 4: the learner does it.t: Your turn: fit it on the manikin, talking me through it. I'll watch.
Step 4: the learner does it.r: Dr Lau keeps in-line stabilisation, takes the earrings off, measures three fingers, sizes, locks and shapes the collar, rear panel then front, checks the fit, then blocks and tape: forehead, then chin. All correct.
Step 4: the learner does it.mark: Peyton step 4: the learner performs while the teacher observes

steps.label: Apply the rule: two cases
steps.hint: He reasons; you ask the questions and confirm.

opts.t: Case one: a 35-year-old, rear-ended at traffic lights, walked about at the scene, now sitting up in the department, GCS 15, sore neck. You talk me through it.
opts.r: No high-risk factor: he's 35, a simple rear-end, no tingling. Low-risk factors: the rear-end, walking, sitting up. So I feel his neck: no midline tenderness. He turns 45 degrees each way: cleared, no imaging.
opts.mark: Has the learner apply the rule to a low-risk case

opts.t: Spot on. And if he couldn't turn 45 degrees?
opts.r: Then he's not cleared: CT his neck.
opts.mark: Probes understanding with a follow-up question

opts.t: Case two: a 72-year-old who tripped and fell from standing, neck pain, GCS 15, no midline tenderness.
opts.r: She's 72: that's high risk on its own. Spinal motion restriction and a CT C-spine, and I don't test her movement at all.
opts.mark: The learner identifies a high-risk factor and does not test movement

opts.t: Exactly: age 65 or over alone means imaging, whatever the examination shows.
opts.mark: Confirms and reinforces the key point

steps.label: Close the session
steps.hint: His view first, then specific feedback, a teach-back, resources and questions.

opts.t: Nearly. Before we finish: how do you think that went?
opts.r: The collar was easier than I thought. The low-risk list is the bit I'm not sure about.

turns.line: The low-risk list is the bit I'm not sure about.

opts.t: You kept the in-line stabilisation the whole time, and your sizing was spot on. For the low-risk factors, ask yourself: is it safe to ask him to move?
You tell me: the three questions of the rule.
opts.r: A high-risk factor: image. No low-risk factor: image. Can't turn 45 degrees: image. Otherwise the neck is cleared.

opts.t: Stiell's original paper from 2001, and NICE guideline NG41. Any questions? Next time we're on together, you clear a neck and I'll watch.
opts.mark: Gives resources, invites questions and agrees a next step

qs.q: Which is a Canadian C-spine Rule high-risk factor?
wrong: A simple rear-end motor vehicle collision
Delayed onset of neck pain after the crash
Able to sit up in the emergency department

qs.q: Which is NOT a NEXUS criterion?
First-line C-spine imaging in an adult who needs it (NICE)?
A dangerous mechanism in the CCR includes…
wrong: Twisting the neck at the gym

qs.q: A harm of a tight collar?

badge.name: Neck Guard
badge.flavor: High risk → image. Low risk → rotate 45°. Can do → clear.

cards.q: Canadian C-spine Rule: which mandates imaging?
cards.why: Age ≥65, dangerous mechanism, or limb paraesthesia.

cards.q: The CCR rotation test requires turning the head…

options: Top of the shoulder to the chin, in finger breadths
Chin to sternal notch, in finger breadths
The patient's height and weight on a chart
cards.why: Match it on the collar from the sizing mark to the bottom of the hard plastic (the foam does not count).

cards.q: First-line C-spine imaging in adults (NICE NG41)?
cards.why: CT is more sensitive and faster in adults.

cards.q: NEXUS requires which to be absent?
cards.why: NEXUS: no midline tenderness, no intoxication, normal alertness, no focal deficit, no painful distracting injury.

options: Motion restriction; collars not routine for all
Rigid collar and long board for every trauma patient
Soft collar for all patients until X-rays are done
No precautions unless a deficit is present
cards.why: Collars have harms; the self-extricating, ambulant patient may not need one.
